newsitem.title: UK: Green issues dominate oil industry thinking - BP.
newsitem.headline: Green issues dominate oil industry thinking - BP.

text.p: Keeping the environment clean is now a bigger headache for the international oil industry than the fear that world oil supplies will dry up any time soon, British Petroleum said.
"The dominant theme of the (last) decade is the realisation that supply is not the problem," BP chief economist Peter Davies told reporters on Wednesday.
"The decade has been a period of transition from an era concerned about scarcity, to an era increasingly concerned about the environment and its capacity to absorb the waste products of energy use."
Davies was presenting the company's annual review of world energy supply and demand trends.
BP figures showed carbon emissions from fossil fuel use grew by 2.8 percent in 1996, marking a sharp acceleration in growth from 1.6 percent the previous year.

"A very substantial proportion of the scientific community believes there is a significant impact on climate change by human activity and the burning of fossil fuels," said BP Oil chief executive Rolf Stomberg.
"We want to join into the dialogue and help ourselves in solving the problem," he added.
But concern for the issues does not yet extend to curbing BP's own output of oil and gas, Stomberg indicated.
"We are by no means a sunset industry," Stomberg said.
The report said energy demand last year, when oil prices hit a post Gulf War high, grew exceptionally fast.

Spurred on by an unusually cold winter in Europe and North America and low oil stocks, overall world energy demand grew by three percent in 1996, more than double the average rate of growth seen over the past ten years.
But demand for oil and gas was easily matched by extra supply.
Oil consumption rose by 2.4 percent in 1996 to 69.55 million barrels a day (bpd) pd, but production rose by 2.9 percent, according to the BP Statistical Review of World Energy 1997.
While gas demand rose by a rapid 4.7 percent to 2,200 billion cubic metres, output rose to the challenge posting a 4.9 percent growth rate.
And once again, the industry found more oil and gas than it used, with proven oil reserves up two percent and gas reserves up one percent.
Advances in drilling technology and lower costs have helped the industry meet new booming demand, Davies said.
Stomberg said BP aimed to boost its production interests in the fast-growing natural gas business and its marketing interests in the East to meet booming Asian demand.
"Eighty percent of demand increases will be outside the core area of our activities...(it is) important to refocus our portfolio -- we're going East," he said.
BP's report showed that Pakistan was the fastest-growing oil market last year at 13.6 percent, followed by Poland at 10.2 percent.
An oil demand growth rate of 7.9 percent helped India overtake France as the world's sixth largest energy market, while South Korea overtook Italy to claim tenth place.
